item.title: Worth More Than the Bookies Combined
item.description:
Worth More Than the Bookies Combined

Prediction markets now have a profit story to match the volume story. In a research report released Friday, PitchBook estimates Kalshi is on course for $1.2 billion in adjusted earnings in 2026, ahead of DraftKings' guidance for the year, on $3.7 billion in gross revenue. Kalshi has already banked $2.4 billion in fee revenue before rebates this year, with records falling regularly since football season began.

The valuations are the headline. PitchBook puts Kalshi at $42.3 billion and Polymarket at $20.6 billion, a combined $62.9 billion, while Flutter and DraftKings together are worth less than $23 billion after their share prices tumbled. The estimates sit just above the roughly $40 billion and $20 billion levels the two exchanges are reportedly raising funds at, and PitchBook says the acceleration in trading volume warrants them.

The gap between the rivals is earnings, not attention. Polymarket's projected 2026 gross revenue is $842 million, with $526.9 million net and just $34.9 million in adjusted earnings, weighed down by running two exchanges, one in the U.S. and one globally. Marketing is the biggest expense at both firms, about 33 percent of Kalshi's revenue, with all of Kalshi's costs adding up to about 60 percent of revenue.

PitchBook expects the lead to widen, then narrow. By 2028 it projects Kalshi gross revenue of $8.5 billion and adjusted earnings of $3 billion, against Polymarket gross revenue of $3.2 billion and earnings of $624.3 million. Even if a court ruling cost them a quarter of U.S. sports contracts, Kalshi would still be worth $25 billion and Polymarket $14.6 billion: hurt, not ruined.

The engine underneath is volume. Kalshi set a record $5.3 billion day on a recent Saturday, a $10 billion weekend, and $25.5 billion across the seven days to October 26, taking $118.4 million in fee revenue that week. Polymarket US set its own record the same Saturday at $811.2 million. The bookies are no longer the biggest business in the room.

Sources: InGame, PitchBook

item.title: Gold Joins the 15-Minute Club: Polymarket's First Market Beyond Crypto
item.description:
Gold Joins the 15-Minute Club: Polymarket's First Market Beyond Crypto

Polymarket's fastest markets no longer stop at crypto. Its 15-minute gold and silver up-or-down markets are now live, the platform's first contracts outside crypto prices, with Chainlink as the official oracle supplying the pricing for every window.

The format is familiar, the asset is not. Traders buy shares on whether gold or silver closes a rolling 15-minute window above or below the level printed at the open. At spot near $3,980 an ounce, even a $20 move inside a window is just half a percent — a volatility contract, not a claim on the metal itself.

The scale behind the launch is the story. Chainlink and Polymarket say the partnership has already settled more than $11 billion in trading volume across Polymarket's 5- and 15-minute crypto markets. That is about 1.24 times LINK's entire market capitalization of about $8.9 billion, with LINK near $11.59 on October 31, up about 4.9 percent in 24 hours.

The crypto machine it extends is relentless: 15-minute markets settle 96 times a day, crypto accounts for $197 million traded in 24 hours on the DeFi Rate board, and Bitcoin finished up in just 49 percent of its last 1,311 Kalshi windows — 642 of them — a near coin flip where price, not direction, decides the trade.

Gold and silver are only the first step. The stated roadmap is more commodities, with equities and foreign exchange to follow, on a Polymarket US venue that operates as a CFTC-regulated designated contract market. The 15-minute club just opened its doors to traditional assets.

Sources: KuCoin, Chainlink, DeFi Rate, CoinGecko

item.title: Two Exchanges, One Point Apart: The Rivals Agree
item.description:
Two Exchanges, One Point Apart: The Rivals Agree

Two rival exchanges, two different trader bases, and almost the same answer. A side-by-side comparison on October 31 matched 10 events listed on both Polymarket and Kalshi, covering 54 outcomes. Across all of them, the average gap was just 1.0 percentage point.

The biggest markets are the tightest. Democrats to win the House are at 94.5 percent on Polymarket and 93.8 percent on Kalshi, a gap of 0.7 points. Democrats to win the Senate are at 71.5 percent against 70.5 percent, a gap of 1.0. A 25-point Fed hike in December is at 70.5 percent against 69.5 percent, also 1.0.

The exceptions prove how narrow the band is. The widest gap in the whole set is Republicans to win the 2028 presidential election, at 34.5 percent on Polymarket and 40.5 percent on Kalshi, 6.0 points apart. U.S. recession by the end of 2026 is next at 6.5 percent against 2.5 percent, and even there the rules differ between the two venues.

In sports the agreement is exact in places. The Buffalo Bills are at 11.5 percent on both exchanges, the Los Angeles Rams at 6.5 percent on both, and Bayern Munich and Arsenal are level on both in the Champions League market.

That is what a maturing market looks like. Different order books, fees and access rules still leave room for a gap, and a gap is not free money. But when two rivals price 54 outcomes within a point on average, the price is no longer one exchange's opinion. It is the consensus.

item.title: Three Exchanges, Three States, One Week: The Industry Sued Back
item.description:
Three Exchanges, Three States, One Week: The Industry Sued Back

For months, the courtroom traffic ran one way: states sued prediction markets. In the last week of October, the exchanges flipped the script. Between October 26 and 27, Nadex, Kalshi and Polymarket US each walked into a different federal court and sued a state of their own.

Polymarket US moved in Louisiana. Its operator, QCX LLC, sued Attorney General Liz Murrill and the Gaming Control Board on October 27 in the Eastern District of Louisiana, case No. 2:26-cv-02482, arguing the Commodity Exchange Act preempts state enforcement and that the state's stance violates the Commerce Clause. The complaint points to a December 5, 2025 advisory calling sports event contracts illegal gambling, and notes the state's 20 sports wagering licenses go first to in-state casino and racetrack licensees.

Kalshi took Missouri the same day. KalshiEX LLC sued Attorney General Catherine Hanaway and the Gaming Commission in the Eastern District of Missouri, case No. 4:26-cv-01860, on a single claim: federal preemption under the Supremacy Clause. Missouri's September 16 cease-and-desist called Kalshi an unlicensed sports wagering platform and gave it 14 extra days to comply; Kalshi will seek a preliminary injunction, and a restraining order if the state will not stand down.

The third front is Utah, where North American Derivatives Exchange, trading as OG.com Prediction Markets, sued Attorney General Derek Brown on October 26 in the District of Utah, case No. 2:26-cv-01056, before Judge David Barlow. A CFTC-designated contract market since 2004, Nadex launched OG.com in February 2026 and raises express, field and conflict preemption. The same week, the United States and the CFTC sued Utah themselves, days after Utah sued Kalshi on October 20, and Kalshi separately sued Louisiana officials on October 23. The CFTC is now battling 10 states in court.

One federal rulebook or fifty state ones is no longer a panel argument. It is being litigated simultaneously by the regulator and by three competing exchanges that agree on almost nothing else.

Sources: RG, CoinDesk
